name: Basil oil (acne)
lead: Basil oil is an essential oil steam-distilled from basil (Ocimum basilicum). European basil oil is high in linalool and methyl chavicol (estragole), roughly 3:1, with smaller amounts of 1,8-cineole, eugenol and myrcene; composition varies with cultivar.[1]

Laboratory studies have found antibacterial and antifungal activity of basil oil, and one in vitro study tested Thai basil oils and micro-emulsions against Propionibacterium acnes (now Cutibacterium acnes), the bacterium linked to acne.[1][2][3] No human trial of basil oil for acne appears among the sources used here.
infobox: Essential oil; topical or in formulations

paras: Basil oil has been reported to be insecticidal, repellent, nematicidal, antibacterial and antifungal in laboratory settings.[1] A 2013 Molecules paper examined basil and rosemary essential oils as antibacterial agents.[3] A 2006 study evaluated Thai basil oils and their micro-emulsion formulas for in vitro activity against P. acnes.[2]

Nanoemulsion formulations of basil oil have been developed and tested for bactericidal activity, and essential oils including basil have been screened for antioxidant and lipoxygenase-inhibitory activity.[4][5] These are laboratory findings and do not establish effects on human skin.

Wikipedia names estragole as a constituent but does not discuss its human safety.[1] Essential oils can be irritating or sensitizing to skin in general, and basil oil's cytotoxicity has been examined in cell lines.[6] No human safety data for acne use are cited here.
No studies found. Related laboratory research is limited to in vitro and non-human work, such as antimicrobial testing against P. acnes.[2]
No community sources are cited for this entry; basil oil is sometimes discussed among natural, complementary acne agents.

card.summary: A plant essential oil with lab antibacterial activity, including against the acne bacterium in vitro; no human acne studies were found.
card.aka: Sweet basil oil, Ocimum basilicum oil
card.note: Only in vitro data; essential oils can irritate skin.

quick.overview:
Basil oil is distilled from Ocimum basilicum and rich in linalool and estragole. It is occasionally discussed as a natural acne agent.

The supporting research is laboratory work, including an in vitro test of Thai basil oils against the acne bacterium; no human acne trial was found.
quick.mechanism: In the lab, constituents such as linalool and eugenol show antimicrobial activity; how this would translate to skin has not been studied in people.
quick.risks: No human safety data for acne use are cited. Essential oils can irritate or sensitize skin, and basil oil has shown cytotoxicity in cell-line studies.
